headline: $25 billion: Meta ordered to pay massive fine over user privacy
summary: A New Mexico judge ruled that the tech giant misled consumers regarding data access and internal policies, following a case linked to the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
details: A judge in New Mexico has ordered Meta Platforms to pay $25 billion after a jury found the company misled consumers. The case stems from allegations that a political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump's 2016 campaign obtained data from millions of Facebook users without consent.

Judge Francis Mathew stated that Facebook's wrongdoing was systematic and went to the heart of its core business practices. While state law initially warranted a penalty of over $219 billion, the judge reduced the final figure to $25 billion.
The lawsuit, filed by the state's attorney general in 2021, followed revelations that Cambridge Analytica harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app.

New Mexico accused Meta of lying about who had access to user data, how it handled hate speech and misinformation, and other internal policies. Jurors found that 26 of 29 statements made by the company were misleading.
The jury determined that Meta committed over 43 million violations of New Mexico's consumer protection laws. Under state law, the penalties will be directed to New Mexico's school system.

Meta had urged the court to cap penalties at $3.45 billion, arguing that the company does not sell user data and that no consumer was proven to be misled. A spokesperson for Meta did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

This is the second major verdict against Meta in New Mexico in six months. A previous trial concluded in March, ordering the company to pay $375 million and $567 million for misleading users about teen safety and mental health.

topic: websites shut down globally due to cyberattack fears
headline_marked: 70% of websites at risk: [[Global sites shut down]] over PHP security flaw
headline: 70% of websites at risk: Global sites shut down over PHP security flaw
summary: Critical vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language allow hackers to enter servers without passwords, prompting governments and businesses worldwide to take sites offline.
details: Two severe security flaws in PHP, a language used by roughly 70% of the world's websites, have forced numerous government agencies and commercial entities to temporarily shut down their sites.
Experts warn that these vulnerabilities could allow cyberattackers to gain full control of servers and access databases without needing a password.
The US National Security Agency (NSA) has urged organizations to update their systems immediately or disconnect risky systems from the internet to prevent unauthorized access.

The PHP Foundation has released an emergency update to fix the flaws, comparing the severity of this issue to the 2014 'Heartbleed' bug, one of the most significant vulnerabilities in software history.
The flaws were discovered using AI models, including OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol and Google's Gemini 4 Argon, marking a milestone where AI can now identify massive internet-wide vulnerabilities.
In France, the Ministry of the Interior shut down local administration websites, including the Paris Police site, following requests from the national cybersecurity agency.
The Netherlands has taken its digital identity service (DigiD), the House of Representatives website, and the National Cybersecurity Center offline as a precaution.
Belgium's Foreign Ministry also temporarily disabled its website, while Australia's cybersecurity agency, the Australian Signals Directorate, reported its own website was among those affected.
caption:
70% of the world's websites use PHP—and a critical flaw just made them all vulnerable to password-less hacking.

Two severe security flaws in PHP, a language used by roughly 70% of the world's websites, have forced numerous government agencies and commercial entities to temporarily shut down their sites.

Experts warn that these vulnerabilities could allow cyberattackers to gain full control of servers and access databases without needing a password.

The US National Security Agency (NSA) has urged organizations to update their systems immediately or disconnect risky systems from the internet to prevent unauthorized access.

The PHP Foundation has released an emergency update to fix the flaws, comparing the severity of this issue to the 2014 'Heartbleed' bug, one of the most significant vulnerabilities in software history.

The flaws were discovered using AI models, including OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol and Google's Gemini 4 Argon, marking a milestone where AI can now identify massive internet-wide vulnerabilities.

In France, the Ministry of the Interior shut down local administration websites, including the Paris Police site, following requests from the national cybersecurity agency.

The Netherlands has taken its digital identity service (DigiD), the House of Representatives website, and the National Cybersecurity Center offline as a precaution.

Belgium's Foreign Ministry also temporarily disabled its website, while Australia's cybersecurity agency, the Australian Signals Directorate, reported its own website was among those affected.
